content: Licorice, also known as liquorice, is derived from the root of the plant Glycyrrhiza glabra. This plant belongs to the legume family, which includes beans and peas, and is native to southern Europe and parts of Asia. It is a perennial herbaceous plant that can grow up to 1 meter in height. Its leaves are pinnate, measuring approximately 7–15 centimeters in length, and consist of 9–17 leaflets. The plant produces flowers that are 0.8–1.2 centimeters long, ranging in color from purple to pale whitish blue, and these flowers are arranged in loose inflorescences. The fruit of the plant is an oblong pod, about 2–3 centimeters long, containing several seeds. It is typically harvested in the autumn, two to three years after planting. Licorice extract is obtained by boiling the root and evaporating most of the water. The name licorice originates from the Ancient Greek words meaning sweet root. The extract is available in both solid and syrup forms. Its primary active compound, glycyrrhizin, is a natural sweetener that is over 50 times sweeter than sucrose and possesses pharmacological properties. The species Glycyrrhiza uralensis contains a higher concentration of glycyrrhizin compared to Glycyrrhiza glabra. Culinary Applications Licorice flavor is widely used in various candies. In the United Kingdom, licorice allsorts are particularly popular, while in continental Europe, stronger and saltier licorice candies are preferred. Many of these candies are flavored with aniseed oil, and the actual licorice content is often minimal. In Yorkshire, England, licorice was first combined with sugar to create sweets similar to those consumed today. In the Netherlands, licorice candy, known as drop, is a popular treat, with some varieties containing aniseed, while others are mixed with mint, menthol, or laurel. A salty version is made by combining licorice with ammonium chloride. Licorice is also used in soft drinks, such as root beer, and in herbal teas to provide a sweet aftertaste. Dutch youth often create dropwater by mixing licorice root and laurel licorice in water, shaking it into a frothy liquid. Additionally, a licorice-based liqueur called dropshot is popular in the Netherlands. In Italy, particularly in the southern regions, and in Spain, licorice is consumed in its natural form. The root is dug up, cleaned, and chewed as a mouth freshener. Unsweetened licorice, made from 100% pure extract, is also popular in Italy, where it is consumed in small, intensely bitter black pieces. In Calabria, a liqueur made from pure licorice extract is a regional specialty. In Syria, licorice is commonly sold as a drink. Dried licorice root can also be chewed as a natural sweet. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Database, black licorice contains approximately 100 calories per ounce (28 grams). In Chinese cuisine, licorice is used as a spice for savory dishes, often to flavor broths and foods simmered in soy sauce. Similar flavors can be found in anise, star anise, tarragon, and fennel. In Egypt, licorice is the main ingredient in a popular soft drink called عرقسوس ('erk-soos'). Medicinal Uses Powdered licorice root has long been recognized as an effective expectorant and has been used for this purpose since ancient times, particularly in Ayurvedic medicine, where it is also incorporated into tooth powders. Modern cough syrups frequently include licorice extract as an ingredient. Licorice has demonstrated potential in treating mouth ulcers and peptic ulcers. For example, the non-prescription treatment CankerMelts uses glycyrrhiza in a dissolving troche to address aphthous ulcers. Licorice also acts as a mild laxative and has antiviral properties, making it useful for conditions such as shingles and herpes (oral, genital, or ophthalmic). Licorice influences the endocrine system due to its isoflavones, which are phytoestrogens. It can reduce serum testosterone levels, although its effect on free testosterone remains unclear. This occurs because licorice inhibits the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, which normally inactivates cortisol in the kidneys. As a result, cortisol levels appear elevated, mimicking the effects of aldosterone excess, even though aldosterone levels remain normal or low. To mitigate these risks, deglycyrrhizinated licorice preparations are available. Licorice also has gastroprotective properties. It increases mucus production and reduces acid secretion in the stomach, which can aid in the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infections and promote the healing of stomach and duodenal ulcers. It may also alleviate symptoms of upset stomach, ileitis, leaky gut syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and Crohn's disease due to its antispasmodic effects on the gastrointestinal tract. Licorice is considered an adaptogen, meaning it helps regulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. It has been used to manage autoimmune conditions such as lupus, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, and allergies to animal dander. In traditional Chinese medicine, licorice is a common ingredient in herbal formulas, where it is believed to harmonize the other components and facilitate their distribution throughout the body's 12 meridians. It is also used to relieve spasmodic coughs. In traditional American herbalism, licorice is included in the Hoxsey anti-cancer formula. Toxicity Excessive consumption of licorice or licorice-based candies can be toxic to the liver and may cause hypokalemia, hypertension, and edema. Most instances of licorice-induced hypertension are linked to the overconsumption of concentrated licorice candies. These effects are generally reversible upon discontinuation of licorice consumption.
